claim: Most vertebrate and plant RNA and small DNA viruses suppress genomic CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies.
source: Most vertebrate and plant RNA and small DNA viruses suppress genomic CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies, apparently mimicking host mRNA composition.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract supported by citations in the introduction to prior literature (Simmonds et al., 2013; Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997).

claim: Artificially increasing CpG/UpA dinucleotides attenuates viruses through an entirely unknown mechanism.
source: Artificially increasing CpG/UpA dinucleotides attenuates viruses through an entirely unknown mechanism.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016) and is a motivation for the current study.

claim: The restriction in E7 replication in mutants with increased CpG/UpA dinucleotides occurred immediately after viral entry.
source: Using the echovirus 7 (E7) model in several cell types, we show that the restriction in E7 replication in mutants with increased CpG/UpA dinucleotides occurred immediately after viral entry, with incoming virions failing to form replication complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 6-8 showing early time point analysis of viral replication.

claim: Incoming virions with increased CpG/UpA dinucleotides fail to form replication complexes.
source: Using the echovirus 7 (E7) model in several cell types, we show that the restriction in E7 replication in mutants with increased CpG/UpA dinucleotides occurred immediately after viral entry, with incoming virions failing to form replication complexes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7 showing reduced formation of replication complexes.

claim: Sequences of CpG/UpA-high virus stocks showed no evidence of increased mutational errors that would render them replication defective.
source: Sequences of CpG/UpA-high virus stocks showed no evidence of increased mutational errors that would render them replication defective, these viral RNAs were not differentially sequestered in cytoplasmic stress granules nor did they induce a systemic antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Table 3 showing comparable mutation frequencies across all virus variants.

claim: CpG/UpA-high viral RNAs were not differentially sequestered in cytoplasmic stress granules.
source: Sequences of CpG/UpA-high virus stocks showed no evidence of increased mutational errors that would render them replication defective, these viral RNAs were not differentially sequestered in cytoplasmic stress granules nor did they induce a systemic antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 9 showing no differential G3BP localization with viral RNA.

claim: CpG/UpA-high viral RNAs did not induce a systemic antiviral state.
source: Sequences of CpG/UpA-high virus stocks showed no evidence of increased mutational errors that would render them replication defective, these viral RNAs were not differentially sequestered in cytoplasmic stress granules nor did they induce a systemic antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by trans-infection experiments in Figure 10 showing no effect on WT virus replication.

claim: Restriction was not mediated through effects on translation efficiency since replicons with high CpG/UpA sequences inserted into a non-coding region were similarly replication defective.
source: Importantly, restriction was not mediated through effects on translation efficiency since replicons with high CpG/UpA sequences inserted into a non-coding region were similarly replication defective.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2-5 showing comparable attenuation in non-coding and coding region mutants, and Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency.

claim: Host-cells possess intrinsic defence pathways that prevent replication of viruses with increased CpG/UpA frequencies independently of codon usage.
source: Host-cells thus possess intrinsic defence pathways that prevent replication of viruses with increased CpG/UpA frequencies independently of codon usage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results showing attenuation independent of translation effects and classical antiviral pathways.

claim: RNA virus genomes possess RNA secondary and tertiary structures that interact with host cell elements.
source: It is increasingly recognised, however, that RNA virus genomes possess a range of other organisational features, such as formation of RNA secondary and tertiary structures that interact with host cell elements, such as ribosomal proteins in viral internal ribosomal entry sites and in the encoding of replication structures such as the cis- active replication element of picornaviruses (Martínez-Salas et al., 2015; Goodfellow et al., 2003; Steil and Barton, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The genomes of RNA viruses are subject to mutational and compositional constraints with substantial variability in G + C content and apparent avoidance of certain dinucleotides such as CpG and UpA.
source: The genomes of RNA viruses are also subject to a range of poorly understood mutational and compositional constraints, with substantial variability in G + C content and the apparent avoidance of certain dinucleotides (the use of two adjacent nucleotides in a linear sequence), such as CpG and UpA (Simmonds et al., 2013; Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature documenting these patterns.

claim: TpA (UpA in RNA) is under-represented in coding sequences of most organisms.
source: In coding sequences of most organisms, TpA (UpA in RNA) is under-represented while vertebrate and plant genomes additionally show strong suppression of CpG dinucleotides (Josse et al., 1961; Russell et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vertebrate and plant genomes show strong suppression of CpG dinucleotides.
source: In coding sequences of most organisms, TpA (UpA in RNA) is under-represented while vertebrate and plant genomes additionally show strong suppression of CpG dinucleotides (Josse et al., 1961; Russell et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UpA dinucleotides in cytoplasmic mRNA and likely also viral RNA are under direct selection as the dinucleotide is recognised by RNA-degrading enzymes in the cytoplasm.
source: UpA dinucleotides in cytoplasmic mRNA and likely also viral RNA are under direct selection as the dinucleotide is recognised by RNA-degrading enzymes in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Duan and Antezana, 2003; Beutler et al., 1989).

claim: The degree of UpA dinucleotides in a RNA molecule has been hypothesized to control cellular RNA turn-over.
source: The degree of UpA dinucleotides in a RNA molecule has therefore been hypothesized to control cellular RNA turn-over (Duan and Antezana, 2003; Beutler et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cytosine in a CpG dinucleotide can be methylated, making it more likely to deaminate into a thymine.
source: A different, enzymatic mechanism underlies the suppression of CpG in host genomes; the cytosine in a CpG dinucleotide can be methylated, making it more likely to deaminate into a thymine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).

claim: DNA methylation selectively reduces CpG dinucleotide frequencies in both plant and vertebrate genomes where DNA methylation is extensive.
source: This selectively reduces CpG dinucleotide frequencies in both plant and vertebrate genomes where DNA methylation is extensive (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most small DNA viruses and viruses with single stranded RNA genomes appear to mimic host-cell mRNA dinucleotide frequencies.
source: Most small DNA viruses and viruses with single stranded RNA genomes appear to mimic host-cell mRNA dinucleotide frequencies, with a strong bias in both UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies in viruses of plants and vertebrates (Simmonds et al., 2013; Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The genome of many invertebrates lack methylation and consequently show little if any suppression of CpG dinucleotide frequencies.
source: In contrast, the genome of many invertebrates lack methylation and consequently show little if any suppression of CpG dinucleotide frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Lobo et al., 2009; Simmonds et al., 2013).

claim: The genomes of viruses that infect invertebrates show little suppression of CpG.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis for virus mimicry, the genomes of viruses that infect invertebrates show little suppression of CpG (Lobo et al., 2009; Simmonds et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways.
source: For example, increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 (E7, enterovirus, Picornaviridae) while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways, whereas removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus.
source: For example, increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 (E7, enterovirus, Picornaviridae) while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways, whereas removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies were entirely non-pathogenic in mice and viral loads were markedly reduced.
source: In mice, infections with influenza virus (Influenzavirus A, Orthomyxoviridae) with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies were entirely non-pathogenic and viral loads were markedly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gaunt et al., 2016).

claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies elicited inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus.
source: Such infections did however elicit inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus and conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus (Gaunt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus.
source: Such infections did however elicit inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus and conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus (Gaunt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Alteration of CpG and UpA frequencies in viruses may introduce normally unfavoured codons or codon pairs that reduce translation rates.
source: Such changes may have the secondary effect of introducing normally unfavoured codons or codon pairs in viral genomes, reducing translation rates that may cause further virus attenuation (Martínez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents a hypothesis being tested in the current study.

claim: In the E7 picornavirus model, dinucleotide frequency changes were the primary factor behind attenuation rather than codon pair bias.
source: When done in the E7 picornavirus model, we found it was dinucleotide frequency changes that were the primary factor behind attenuation (Tulloch et al., 2014), although this conclusion has been disputed (Futcher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors, though noted as disputed.

claim: Upon entry into the host cell the viral genomic RNA of E7 is quickly released into the cytoplasm.
source: Upon entry into the host cell the viral genomic RNA is quickly released into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claim: E7 viral RNA is translated through a cap-independent mechanism into a single polyprotein that is further processed.
source: Through a cap-independent mechanism viral RNA is translated into a single polyprotein that is further processed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claim: E7 RNA replication occurs in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) associated vesicles.
source: RNA replication occurs in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) associated vesicles, where from a negative-sense RNA intermediate progeny positive-sense RNA genomes are transcribed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claim: The dsRNA replication intermediate is a known activator of cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, such as RIG-I and MDA5.
source: The dsRNA replication intermediate is a known activator of cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, such as retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) (Baum et al., 2010; Peisley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The induction and secretion of interferon induces expression of a large number of cellular genes whose expression leads to the induction of an antiviral state within the cell.
source: The consequent induction and secretion of interferon induces expression of a large number of cellular genes whose expression leads to the induction of an antiviral state within the cell (Randall and Goodbourn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Viral titres of E7 with R2_U or R2_C were consistently lower compared to WT E7 across different cell types.
source: Twenty-four hours post infection with the E7 R2 mutant viruses, infectious progeny virus was measured with an end point dilution assay (EPDA). Across the different cell types, the viral titres of E7 with R2_U or R2_C were consistently lower compared to WT E7 (Figure 1B, one-way ANOVA, p<0.01,).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: The relative replication rates (RRRs) of E7 mutants differed between cell types.
source: The relative replication rates (RRRs; ratio of TCID50s of mutant/WT virus) of E7 mutants differed between cell types.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing different RRR values across cell lines.

claim: In RD cells R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1.
source: In RD cells (human muscle) and A549 cells (human lung epithelium) R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1 and 0.4 respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: In A549 cells R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.4.
source: In RD cells (human muscle) and A549 cells (human lung epithelium) R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1 and 0.4 respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The RRR of R2_C was 0.01 in RD and A549 cells.
source: The RRR of R2_C was further suppressed to 0.01 in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells that originated from the kidney displayed a more moderate E7 R2_C RRR of approximately 0.09.
source: Cells that originated from the kidney displayed a more moderate E7 R2_C RRR of approximately 0.09 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no relationship between RRR and virus titre of WT virus at 24 hr.
source: However, there was no relationship between RRR (Figure 1C, x-axis) and virus titre of WT virus at 24 hr (Figure 1C, y-axis, representing cell susceptibility; Pearson correlation coefficient CpG −0.57 and UpA −0.63).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A549 cells expressing BVDV NPro showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
source: These included A549 cells expressing the bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV, genus Pestivirus) N-terminal protease fragment (NPro), which blocks the activity of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF-3)(Hilton et al., 2006) and IRF7 (Fiebach et al., 2011) or the hepatitis C virus (HCV, genus Hepacivirus) protein NS3/4A that inhibits cytokine gene expression by cleavage of IPS-1/MAVS/VISA/Cardif (Kaukinen et al., 2006). Both cell lines showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing RRR values for A549-Npro cells.

claim: A549 cells expressing HCV NS3/4A showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
source: These included A549 cells expressing the bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV, genus Pestivirus) N-terminal protease fragment (NPro), which blocks the activity of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF-3)(Hilton et al., 2006) and IRF7 (Fiebach et al., 2011) or the hepatitis C virus (HCV, genus Hepacivirus) protein NS3/4A that inhibits cytokine gene expression by cleavage of IPS-1/MAVS/VISA/Cardif (Kaukinen et al., 2006). Both cell lines showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing RRR values for A549 NS3/4A cells.

claim: Vero cells restricted mutated E7 viruses comparable to that of other cultured kidney cells tested with a more moderate attenuation of the CpG high virus.
source: The monkey kidney fibroblast cell line, Vero, which has intact IFN signalling pathways but cannot produce type 1 IFNs (Desmyter et al., 1968), restricted mutated E7 viruses comparable to that of other cultured kidney cells tested in this study with a more moderate attenuation between of the CpG high virus (Figure 1BC).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types.
source: Together this indicates that reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types and restriction cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 1 showing consistent attenuation across cell types.

claim: Restriction of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
source: Together this indicates that reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types and restriction cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
evidence: This is supported by data showing attenuation persists in cells with inhibited IRF3 and MAVS pathways (Figure 1B).

claim: A permutated mutant of E7, with the native sequences of R1 or R2 scrambled but retaining coding and native dinucleotide frequencies, showed WT levels of replication.
source: This was supported by a high synonymous site variability and low mean folding energies (Atkinson et al., 2014). In these experiments a permutated mutant of E7, with the native sequences of R1 or R2 scrambled but retaining coding and native dinucleotide frequencies, showed WT levels of replication, indicative that these genome region can be safely modified without consequences for viral replication (Atkinson et al., 2014; Tulloch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Synonymous removal of all possible CpG and UpA dinucleotides from firefly luciferase strongly increased the replication rate of the E7luc replicon.
source: Being of insect origin, the wild type firefly luciferase gene (luc_WT) contains a relatively high ratio of CpG dinucleotides (CpG 1.210 and UpA 0.695 observed/expected). Synonymous removal of all possible CpG and UpA dinucleotides from firefly luciferase (luc_cu, ratio CpG 0.013 and UpA 0.154 O/E) strongly increased the replication rate of the E7luc replicon (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of the 1242 nucleotide long ncR1 of WT composition to the E7 replicon RNA had no effect on replication compared to that of the E7 replicon without ncR1.
source: Addition of the 1242 nucleotide long ncR1 of WT composition to the E7 replicon RNA had no effect on replication compared to that of the E7 replicon without ncR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The replication structures in the 3'-UTR are not affected by the addition of 1242 nucleotides to the 5'-end of the 3'-UTR.
source: This indicates that the replication structures in the 3'-UTR are not affected by the addition of 1242 nucleotides to the 5'-end of the 3'-UTR.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that adding ncR1 does not affect replication.

claim: RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5).
source: However, RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail (ncR1_U) in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5), whereas the high CpG sequence, ncR1_C, reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection (hpt) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: The high CpG sequence ncR1_C reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection.
source: However, RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail (ncR1_U) in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5), whereas the high CpG sequence, ncR1_C, reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection (hpt) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar degrees of attenuation were observed in replicons where CpG and UpA frequencies were increased through mutation of the coding region in R2.
source: Similar degrees of attenuation were observed in replicons where CpG and UpA frequencies were increased through mutation of the coding region in R2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B comparing coding and non-coding region mutants.

claim: The RRRs of both coding and non-coding CpG- and UpA-mutants approached that of WT in kidney-derived BHK cells.
source: In contrast, the RRRs of both coding and non-coding CpG- and UpA-mutants approached that of WT in kidney-derived BHK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No effects on replication were observed in replicons with ncR1 (non-coding) or R2 (coding) sequences possessing lower (cu) CpG/UpA frequencies than WT.
source: No effects on replication were observed in replicons with ncR1 (non-coding) or R2 (coding) sequences possessing lower (cu) CpG/UpA frequencies than WT (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Kinase inhibitor C16 was able to largely reverse the attenuation of CpG- and UpA-high mutants of E7 virus, independently of PKR.
source: We previously reported that kinase inhibitor C16 was able to largely reverse the attenuation of CpG- and UpA-high mutants of E7 virus, independently of PKR (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The relative luciferase expression of E7 replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotides in their ncR1 were increased by 1.8 and 6 fold respectively in the presence of C16.
source: The relative luciferase expression of E7 replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotides in their ncR1 were increased by 1.8 and 6 fold respectively in the presence of C16 while the replication of WT and CDLR was unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, p-values 0.069 and 0.01, T-test).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: The observed reversal of attenuation of the E7 ncR1 variants by C16 closely resembled that of viruses with modifications in the coding region.
source: The observed reversal of attenuation of the E7 ncR1 variants closely resembled that of viruses with modifications in the coding region (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and provides evidence that the mechanisms of attenuation in the two systems were similar.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 comparing replicons and viruses.

claim: The replicon with ncR1_C showed an RRR of approximately 0.1 in A549 and RD cells.
source: The replicon with ncR1_C showed an RRR of approximately 0.1 in A549 and RD cells, a greater degree of attenuation than observed in the kidney-derived 293, 293T and Vero cells, while attenuation in the pathway knockout cells, A549-V and A549 NS3/4A was greater (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: The ranking of cell lines for attenuation of both CpG and UpA-elevated mutants was similar between the virus and replicon challenge systems.
source: Although the overall degree of attenuation in the replicon format was lower than in the low MOI infection experiments performed for infectious virus (Figure 1B), the ranking of cell lines for attenuation of both CpG and UpA-elevated mutants was similar between the two challenge systems (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figures 1B and 3B.

claim: In all murine cell types, replication rates of replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies in the non-coding region were consistently lower than WT.
source: At six hpt, samples were lysed and assayed for luciferase expression. In all cell types replication rates of replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies in the non-coding region were consistently lower than WT (RRRs ranging from 0.01 to 0.3 for ncR1_C and 0.2–0.7 for ncR1_U).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Replicon mutants with an ncR1 of P or cu composition invariably showed equivalent replication to WT in murine cells.
source: In contrast, replicon mutants with an ncR1 of P or cu composition invariably showed equivalent replication to WT (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: GuHCl effectively inhibits picornavirus RNA replication through inhibiting initiation of negative strand RNA synthesis and RNA strand elongation.
source: It is well established that GuHCl effectively inhibits picornavirus RNA replication through inhibiting initiation of negative strand RNA synthesis and RNA strand elongation (Barton and Flanegan, 1997; Pfister and Wimmer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GuHCl treatment or mutation of the viral polymerase similarly reduced luciferase readings throughout the time-course experiment, with no sign of replicon RNA replication.
source: GuHCl treatment or mutation of the viral polymerase similarly reduced luciferase readings throughout the time-course experiment, with no sign of replicon RNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: E7 replicons with CpG or UpA high ncR1 showed comparable luciferase expression as replicons with WT ncR1 sequences when replication was inhibited by either GuHCl or mutation of the viral polymerase.
source: Importantly, E7 replicons with CpG or UpA high ncR1 showed comparable luciferase expression as replicons with WT ncR1 sequences when replication was inhibited by either GuHCl or mutation of the viral polymerase (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C showing no difference in translation between WT and mutant replicons when replication is blocked.

claim: Untreated, replication competent replicons displayed the typical attenuation of luciferase expression in CpG and UpA mutants.
source: Untreated, replication competent replicons displayed the typical attenuation of luciferase expression in CpG and UpA mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a modest, approximate 5-fold reduction in luciferase expression over the 24 hr course of the experiment observed in non-replicating replicons that may reflect partial degradation of the transfected RNA.
source: There was a modest, approximate 5-fold reduction in luciferase expression over the 24 hr course of the experiment observed in non-replicating replicons that may reflect partial degradation of the transfected RNA.
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 4B and 4C showing declining luciferase over time in non-replicating conditions.

claim: Reductions in luciferase expression were comparable between WT and CpG/UpA modified replicons in non-replicating conditions.
source: Reductions in luciferase expression were comparable between WT and CpG/UpA modified replicons (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C showing similar decay rates.

claim: At six hours post transfection, replicating E7 replicon RNA with a CpG-high ncR1 displayed an approximate 10-fold reduction in luciferase expression when compared to WT.
source: At six hours post transfection, replicating E7 replicon RNA with a CpG-high ncR1 displayed an approximate 10-fold reduction in luciferase expression when compared to WT (Figure 4D, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: When replication was inhibited by GuHCl, translation from the CpG-high replicon RNA was comparable to that of the WT in all tested cell types.
source: In contrast, when replication was inhibited by GuHCl, translation from the CpG-high replicon RNA was comparable to that of the WT in all tested cell types (Figure 4D, black bars).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4D showing similar translation efficiency when replication is blocked.

claim: Replicons with UpA-modified ncR1 also expressed similar levels of luciferase compared to WT in a non-replicating context with ratios ranging from 0.5 to 2.9.
source: Replicons with UpA-modified ncR1 also expressed similar levels of luciferase compared to WT in a non-replicating context with ratios ranging from 0.5 to 2.9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed attenuation of UpA or CpG high replicon mutants is not dependent on differences in translation rates or instability of the coding region RNA sequences in the cell.
source: Combined, these results demonstrate that the observed attenuation of UpA or CpG high replicon mutants is not dependent on differences in translation rates or instability of the coding region RNA sequences in the cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency between WT and mutant replicons when replication is blocked.

claim: Replicons with the single CpG-high ncS showed significantly reduced E7 RNA replication.
source: Transfection of these replicon RNAs with various compositions in their ncS regions into RD cells resulted in significantly reduced E7 RNA replication for the single CpG-high ncS (ncS_C) but not the single UpA-high ncS_U (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Replicons with the single UpA-high ncS did not show significantly reduced E7 RNA replication.
source: Transfection of these replicon RNAs with various compositions in their ncS regions into RD cells resulted in significantly reduced E7 RNA replication for the single CpG-high ncS (ncS_C) but not the single UpA-high ncS_U (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Replicons with the double ncS of both U and C composition showed significantly reduced replication compared to their respective single ncS replicons.
source: However replicons with the double ncS of both U and C composition showed significantly reduced replication compared to their respective single ncS replicons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Luciferase expression of the CpG-high double region mutant was little different from that of the non-replicative guanidine treated control, indicating that this longer insertion almost entirely abrogated replication of this construct.
source: Indeed, luciferase expression of the CpG-high double region mutant was little different from that of the non-replicative guanidine treated control (Figure 5B; dotted red line), indicating that this longer insertion almost entirely abrogated replication of this construct.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B comparing double CpG mutant to GuHCl control.

claim: Cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs.
source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: CpG/UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting.
source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency.

claim: Codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: The restriction mechanism implies a cell-mediated restriction of viral RNA replication and/or an alternative fate of the compositionally altered (viral) RNA.
source: Rather it implies a cell-mediated restriction of viral RNA replication and/or an alternative fate of the compositionally altered (viral) RNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing restriction independent of translation effects.

claim: Infection with equal RNA resulted in reduced infectivity of E7 R2_C virus as early as two hours post infection.
source: Infection with equal RNA resulted in reduced infectivity of E7 R2_C virus as early as two hours post infection and a prolonged delay in the production of progeny virus and RNA levels (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6A showing reduced viral titers at early time points.

claim: There was no difference in initial receptor binding/viral entry between the E7 variant R2_C and other mutants as the genomic RNA copies detected after washing off the inoculum were identical to the mean of all samples at 1 hr post infection.
source: In this experiment there was no difference in initial receptor binding/viral entry between the E7 variant R2_C and other mutants as the genomic RNA copies detected after washing off the inoculum were identical to the mean of all samples at 1 hr post infection (mean 1.00, R2_C 1.00, R2_U 1.03 SD 0.04).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing equal RNA levels at 1 hpi.

claim: After the initial delay in RNA replication, E7 with increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies replicated at a rate similar to that of other E7 variants.
source: Interestingly, after the initial delay in RNA replication, E7 with increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies replicated at a rate similar to that of other E7 variants (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B showing similar slopes after the initial delay.

claim: Small localized foci with intracellular genomic E7 RNA were observed at two hpi in all infected cells at frequencies that were comparable between WT and mutant viruses.
source: Small localized foci with intracellular genomic E7 RNA were observed at two hpi (Figure 7A, white arrowheads) in all infected cells at frequencies that were comparable between WT and mutant viruses.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7A.

claim: At four hours post infection, WT and R2_U mutants developed clear pockets of replication in a large percentage of cells, whereas detection of E7 RNA with increased CpG dinucleotides became less frequent.
source: At four hours post infection, WT and R2_U mutants developed clear pockets of replication in a large percentage of cells, whereas detection of E7 RNA with increased CpG dinucleotides became less frequent.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7A.

claim: At six hours, RNA replication of E7 R2_C had progressed to display similar fluorescent intensities compared to the other E7 variants, but only in 3.5% of cells, compared to 49% and 36% of cells infected with R2_WT or R2_U viruses, respectively.
source: At six hours, RNA replication of E7 R2_C had progressed to display similar fluorescent intensities compared to the other E7 variants, but only in 3.5% of cells, compared to 49% and 36% of cells infected with R2_WT or R2_U viruses, respectively (Figure 7BC).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RNA FISH data in Figure 7C.

claim: Dinucleotide frequency changes influenced the frequency of infected cells, but not necessarily their subsequent replication ability.
source: The striking observation that dinucleotide frequency changes influenced the frequency of infected cells, but not necessarily their subsequent replication ability was verified by flow cytometry of a further set of E7 replicon constructs in which the luciferase gene was replaced by enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP).
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA FISH data in Figure 7 and verified by FACS data in Figure 8.

claim: FACS analysis showed that the percentage of EGFP expressing cells at 6 hpt differed dramatically between WT and CpG-high mutant replicons while the mean fluorescent intensities of the cells that were fluorescent was comparable.
source: Similar to the above RNA FISH experiments, FACS analysis showed that the percentage of EGFP expressing cells at 6 hpt differed dramatically between WT and CpG-high mutant replicons while the mean fluorescent intensities of the cells that were fluorescent was comparable (Figure 8AB, Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 8A and 8B and Table 2.

claim: Attenuation was enhanced for CpG- and UpA-high mutants when both coding R2 and ncR1 were modified.
source: Attenuation was enhanced for CpG- and UpA-high mutants when both coding R2 and ncR1 were modified (Figure 8 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 8 and Table 2 showing additive effects.

claim: Transfection of replicons with either R2 or ncR1 of UpA and CpG high composition into BHK cells resulted in EGFP expression more similar to WT replicons.
source: Similar to E7 replicons that expressed luciferase, transfection of replicons with either R2 or ncR1 of UpA and CpG high composition into BHK cells resulted in EGFP expression more similar to WT replicons, though replicons with both regions mutated did show a marked reduction in EGFP expression (Figure 8CD, Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: While entry of E7 WT, UpA- and CpG-high mutants was unaffected, replication of these mutants was profoundly restricted at early time points during the replication cycle.
source: Together, this indicates that while entry of E7 WT, UpA- and CpG-high mutants was unaffected, replication of these mutants was profoundly restricted at early time points during the replication cycle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data in Figures 6-8.

claim: In a small number of cells, E7 CpG-high and UpA-high mutants were able to overcome restriction.
source: However, in a small number of cells, E7 CpG-high and UpA-high mutants were able to overcome restriction, suggesting that increasing CpG and UpA dinucleotides renders a large proportion of E7 RNA replication defective or E7 replication is able to counteract or saturate supposed intracellular restriction factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that some cells do show productive replication (Figures 7 and 8).

claim: Increasing CpG and UpA dinucleotides renders a large proportion of E7 RNA replication defective or E7 replication is able to counteract or saturate supposed intracellular restriction factors.
source: However, in a small number of cells, E7 CpG-high and UpA-high mutants were able to overcome restriction, suggesting that increasing CpG and UpA dinucleotides renders a large proportion of E7 RNA replication defective or E7 replication is able to counteract or saturate supposed intracellular restriction factors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that some cells overcome restriction.

claim: Multiple clones from each PCR product of E7 virus stocks showed comparable misincorporation frequencies in the R2 variant viruses.
source: Multiple clones from each PCR product were sequenced and differences from the cloned mutated region recorded (Table 3). For each, RNA from three biological replicates of WT and all four mutant virus stocks showed comparable misincorporation frequencies in the R2 variant viruses.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Table 3.

claim: The average mutation rate of approximately 10−4 mutations/nucleotide closely resembled that of previously published mutation frequency for poliovirus.
source: The average mutation rate of approximately 10−4mutations/nucleotide closely resembled that of previously published mutation frequency for poliovirus (9−5[Sanjuán et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited literature and data in Table 3.

claim: These viral RNAs are not intrinsically replication defective.
source: These results indicate that these viral RNAs are not intrinsically replication defective.
evidence: This is an inference from the sequencing data showing no increased mutation rates.

claim: The observation that fitness defects in both UpA and CpG-high mutant viruses and replicons can be reversed by kinase inhibitor C16 provides further evidence that the nature of the replication defect is not caused by increased mutation rates.
source: The observation that fitness defects in both UpA and CpG-high mutant viruses and replicons can be reversed by kinase inhibitor C16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) provides further evidence that the nature of the replication defect is not caused by increased mutation rates.
evidence: This is an inference from the C16 reversal data and sequencing data.

claim: The inhibition in replication of incoming RNA with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies is the result of host-cell restriction factors.
source: Together, this suggests that the inhibition in replication of incoming RNA with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies is the result of host-cell restriction factors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined evidence ruling out intrinsic defects.

claim: Regardless of the nucleotide composition of the incoming viruses (WT, C, U), no typical G3BP positive cytoplasmic granules corresponding to those found in uninfected sodium arsenite treated samples were observed during infection with E7.
source: Regardless of the nucleotide composition of the incoming viruses (WT, C, U), no typical G3BP positive cytoplasmic granules corresponding to those found in uninfected sodium arsenite treated samples were observed during infection with E7, nor did G3BP localize with E7 genomic RNA (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 9.

claim: G3BP did not localize with E7 genomic RNA.
source: Regardless of the nucleotide composition of the incoming viruses (WT, C, U), no typical G3BP positive cytoplasmic granules corresponding to those found in uninfected sodium arsenite treated samples were observed during infection with E7, nor did G3BP localize with E7 genomic RNA (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 9.

claim: Infection with the E7 UpA and CpG high variants at either equal infectivity or equal RNA did not result in a considerable increase in eIF2α phosphorylation compared to infection with WT E7 or the permutated control.
source: Infection with the E7 UpA and CpG high variants at either equal infectivity or equal RNA did not result in a considerable increase ineIF2α phosphorylation compared to infection with WT E7 or the permutated control (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of cells with ACF did not change the RRR of E7luc replicons with ncR1 variants from their respective DMSO treated controls.
source: However, treatment of cells with ACF did not change the RRR of E7luc replicons with ncR1 variants from their respective DMSO treated controls (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Caspase 3/7 activity levels correlated with viral replication rates rather than with CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies.
source: Levels correlated with viral replication rates rather than with CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies, providing strong evidence that the reduced replication of viruses with increased genomic UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies was not caused by an increased induction of programmed cell death (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by caspase assay data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced replication of viruses with increased genomic UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies was not caused by an increased induction of programmed cell death.
source: Levels correlated with viral replication rates rather than with CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies, providing strong evidence that the reduced replication of viruses with increased genomic UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies was not caused by an increased induction of programmed cell death (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference from the caspase assay data.

claim: Viruses with increased CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies do not differentially induce stress, interferon-coupled or apoptosis-associated antiviral pathways.
source: Together, this suggests that viruses with increased CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies do not differentially induce stress, interferon-coupled or apoptosis-associated antiviral pathways and that none of these can be plausibly attributed as mediations of their restricted replication phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data in Figure 9 and supplements.

claim: None of the tested antiviral pathways can be plausibly attributed as mediations of the restricted replication phenotypes of CpG/UpA-high mutants.
source: Together, this suggests that viruses with increased CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies do not differentially induce stress, interferon-coupled or apoptosis-associated antiviral pathways and that none of these can be plausibly attributed as mediations of their restricted replication phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined negative results for various antiviral pathways.

claim: Titres of the superinfecting WT virus were similar between all samples and therefore entirely unaffected by the nucleotide composition of the R2 RNA co-expressed in these cells.
source: However, titres of the superinfecting WT virus were similar between all samples and therefore entirely unaffected by the nucleotide composition of the R2 RNA co-expressed in these cells (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10A showing no trans effect.

claim: Luciferase expression of the E7 replicon was not affected by co-transfected ncS RNAs, regardless of their dinucleotide frequencies.
source: At six hpt, cells were lysed and luciferase expression was measured. Luciferase expression of the E7 replicon was not affected by co-transfected ncS RNAs, regardless of their dinucleotide frequencies (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10B showing no trans effect.

claim: Luciferase expression of the co-transfected reporter replicon was unaffected by the dinucleotide composition of co-transfected interfering replicons.
source: In contrast to the effects dinucleotide frequencies have on viral RNA replication in cis, luciferase expression of the co-transfected reporter replicon was unaffected (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10C showing no trans effect.

claim: Neither replicating viral RNA nor non-replicating RNA sequences in the cytoplasm with elevated CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies had any detectable trans effect on E7 replication.
source: Together, these findings indicate that neither replicating viral RNA nor non-replicating RNA sequences in the cytoplasm with elevated CpG or UpA dinucleotide frequencies had any detectable trans effect on E7 replication.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data in Figure 10.

claim: The strict restriction on replication in cis demonstrates that expression of RNAs with elevated CpG or UpA frequencies mediates a quite different form of replication inhibition than the antiviral state induced by stress pathways or IFN-β induction through activation of conventional PRRs.
source: The strict restriction on replication in cis demonstrates that expression of RNAs with elevated CpG or UpA frequencies mediates a quite different form of replication inhibition than the antiviral state induced by stress pathways or IFN-β induction through activation of conventional PRRs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of trans effects and the cis-specific restriction.

claim: Higher G + C content generally allows for a higher frequency of CpG dinucleotides in naturally occurring sequences.
source: However, the suppression of CpG dinucleotides is composition dependent. Higher G + C content generally allows for a higher frequency of CpG dinucleotides in naturally occurring sequences (Fryxell and Moon, 2005; Simmonds et al., 2013), including isolates of the enterovirus genus (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and data in Figure 11A.

claim: The ncR1_AACGAA showed an RRR comparable to that of the CpG-high sequence (containing 181 CpG dinucleotides).
source: Despite these mutants possessing the WT number of CpG dinucleotides, their replication was profoundly impaired (Figure 11B); the ncR1_AACGAA showed an RRR comparable to that of the CpG-high sequence (containing 181 CpG dinucleotides).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11B.

claim: The replication of the ncR1_UUCGUU was further impaired with an RRR 30-fold lower than the WT control of identical CpG content.
source: Remarkably, the replication of the ncR1_UUCGUU was further impaired with an RRR 30-fold lower than the WT control of identical CpG content.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 11B.

claim: The context of the bases surrounding the CpG dinucleotide has a potent effect on replication attenuation.
source: The context of the bases surrounding the CpG dinucleotide has a potent effect on replication attenuation.
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 11B showing differential attenuation based on CpG context.

claim: CpG and UpA dinucleotides are under-represented in the genomes of most RNA viruses infecting vertebrates and plants.
source: CpG and UpA dinucleotides are under-represented in the genomes of most RNA viruses infecting vertebrates and plants (Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997; Simmonds et al., 2013) but the host factors or mutational mechanisms that impose this suppression in viral genomic nucleotide compositions are still unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The host factors or mutational mechanisms that impose suppression of CpG and UpA in viral genomic nucleotide compositions are still unknown.
source: CpG and UpA dinucleotides are under-represented in the genomes of most RNA viruses infecting vertebrates and plants (Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997; Simmonds et al., 2013) but the host factors or mutational mechanisms that impose this suppression in viral genomic nucleotide compositions are still unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The functional constraints act directly on RNA with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotides to inhibit viral RNA replication.
source: Here we characterise mechanistically how the viral replication cycle is affected by increased genomic CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies in viral genomes and narrow down the possible cellular processes involved. Importantly we show that the functional constraints act directly on RNA with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotides to inhibit viral RNA replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: The functional constraints on CpG/UpA-high RNA occur independent of whether these nucleotides are in coding or non-coding RNA.
source: This occurs independent of whether these nucleotides are in coding or non-coding RNA and without induction of a systemic, cell-wide antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing coding and non-coding region mutants (Figures 2-5).

claim: The functional constraints on CpG/UpA-high RNA occur without induction of a systemic, cell-wide antiviral state.
source: This occurs independent of whether these nucleotides are in coding or non-coding RNA and without induction of a systemic, cell-wide antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by trans-infection experiments showing no antiviral state (Figure 10).

claim: The similarity in pattern of RRR observed in different cell lines between E7 virus and replicons, and their shared responsiveness to C16 corroborates the use of this replicon system with non-coding sequence variants.
source: The similarity in pattern of RRR observed in different cell lines between E7 virus and replicons, and their shared responsiveness to C16 corroborates the use of this replicon system with non-coding sequence variants.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of virus and replicon data.

claim: The data reported in the current study reinforces the conclusion that attenuation associated with unfavoured codon pairs originates from unintentional increase in CpG and UpA dinucleotides.
source: The data reported in the current study reinforces this conclusion, at least for the echovirus seven model we used, by demonstrating that replication rates were similarly affected by addition of CpG and UpA dinucleotides in the 3' non-coding region as they were in the coding part of the genome (Figures 2, 5 and 8).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of coding and non-coding region effects.

claim: CpG- and UpA-induced attenuation must be mainly mediated in a manner that is independent of codon usage or codon pair bias.
source: CpG- and UpA-induced attenuation therefore must be mainly mediated in a manner that is independent of codon usage or codon pair bias.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that non-coding region mutants show similar attenuation.

claim: Translation efficiency is very clearly a potential additional factor that may influence virus replication rates for viruses that have different replication mechanisms to E7.
source: These observations were however restricted to the echovirus model, and while they may also underlie the observed attenuation of other viruses with codon or codon pair de-optimised coding regions, translation efficiency is very clearly a potential additional factor that may influence virus replication rates, and does not exclude the existence of additional mechanisms that may attenuate viruses based on codon or codon pair choice, particularly for viruses that have different replication mechanisms to E7.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the findings to other viruses.

claim: The apparent necessity for under-representation of UpA and CpG dinucleotides in viral RNA is one element that has contributed to biases in nucleotide composition and as a result the choice of codons and codon pairs in native viral sequences.
source: The findings do suggest, however, that the apparent necessity for under-representation of UpA and CpG dinucleotides in viral RNA is one element that has contributed to biases in nucleotide composition and as a result the choice of codons and codon pairs in native viral sequences.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: The importance of the current study is that we can at least for the E7 model, entirely disentangle the effects of dinucleotide frequency modification from translation efficiency.
source: The importance of the current study is that we can at least for the E7 model, entirely disentangle the effects of dinucleotide frequency modification from translation efficiency and produce experimental findings that complement conclusions reached previously using other viruses and other experimental approaches (Burns et al., 2006; Burns et al., 2009; Tulloch et al., 2014; Kunec and Osterrieder, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study's findings.

claim: The marked phenotypic effect arose because the initial replication entities of CpG-high viruses failed to progress to form the larger replication complexes observed in WT and also most UpA-high infected cells.
source: The marked phenotypic effect arose because the initial replication entities of CpG-high viruses failed to progress to form the larger replication complexes observed in WT and also most UpA-high infected cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA FISH data in Figure 7.

claim: Once formed, replication complexes from CpG-high viruses showed comparable levels of viral RNA by RNA-FISH.
source: Once formed, replication complexes from CpG-high viruses showed comparable levels of viral RNA by RNA-FISH.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7 showing similar fluorescence intensity in positive cells.

claim: The reduction in replication competent particles could be the result of post-transcriptional RNA-editing of the viral genome that rendered them replication defective.
source: This reduction in replication competent particles could be the result of post-transcriptional RNA-editing of the viral genome that rendered them replication defective.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested and ruled out by sequencing data.

claim: APOBEC editing substantially limits the replication ability of HIV-1 and other retroviruses.
source: APOBEC editing substantially limits the replication ability of HIV-1 and other retroviruses; so powerfully indeed that many retroviruses have developed specific antagonism pathways, such as Vif in HIV-1 that limits APOBEC's effect (Hultquist et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There was no evidence of a specific RNA editing signature among the identified mutations in E7 virus stocks.
source: There was also no evidence of a specific RNA editing signature among the identified mutations (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Table 3.

claim: The observed failure of CpG-high viruses to initiate replication is not the result of genomic sequences being defective.
source: The observed failure of CpG-high viruses to initiate replication is therefore not the result of genomic sequences being defective.
evidence: This is an inference from the sequencing data showing no increased mutation rates.

claim: UpA and CpG dinucleotides are self-complementary and may increase the likelihood of intramolecular base pairing, which could impact the efficiency of the viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase.
source: UpA and CpG dinucleotides are self-complementary and may increase the likelihood of intramolecular base pairing, which could impact the efficiency of the viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (Lai, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The reversal of the restricted replication phenotypes of CpG- and UpA-high mutants by the kinase inhibitor C16 argues strongly against the existence of an intrinsic replication defect in the mutant viruses.
source: However, the reversal of the restricted replication phenotypes of CpG- and UpA-high mutants by the kinase inhibitor C16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and the reduction in their attenuation in BHK and other kidney cells lines (Figures 1–3 and 8) argues strongly against the existence of an intrinsic replication defect in the mutant viruses.
evidence: This is an inference from the C16 reversal data.

claim: The reduction in attenuation of CpG/UpA-high mutants in BHK and other kidney cells lines argues strongly against the existence of an intrinsic replication defect in the mutant viruses.
source: However, the reversal of the restricted replication phenotypes of CpG- and UpA-high mutants by the kinase inhibitor C16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and the reduction in their attenuation in BHK and other kidney cells lines (Figures 1–3 and 8) argues strongly against the existence of an intrinsic replication defect in the mutant viruses.
evidence: This is an inference from the cell line comparison data.

claim: CpG- or UpA- elevation in a non-functional genome region led to a similar attenuation as observed in coding region mutants.
source: This conclusion is reinforced by the observation that CpG- or UpA- elevation in a non-functional genome region (the 3' ncR1 or ncS) led to a similar attenuation as observed in coding region mutants (Figures 2, 3 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: The structure and configuration of viral genomic RNA may serve as PAMPs for interferon pathway-coupled PRRs.
source: It is known that the structure and configuration of viral genomic RNA may serve as PAMPs for interferon pathway-coupled PRRs (Yoneyama et al., 2016; Oshiumi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UpA and UpU dinucleotides in viral RNAs can be cleaved by RNase L.
source: UpA and UpU dinucleotides in viral RNAs can be cleaved by RNase L (Cooper et al., 2015, 2014) and produce 5' phosphorylated RNA termini that activate RIG-I mediated IFN-β expression (Malathi et al., 2007; Malathi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNase L cleavage products produce 5' phosphorylated RNA termini that activate RIG-I mediated IFN-β expression.
source: UpA and UpU dinucleotides in viral RNAs can be cleaved by RNase L (Cooper et al., 2015, 2014) and produce 5' phosphorylated RNA termini that activate RIG-I mediated IFN-β expression (Malathi et al., 2007; Malathi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNase L cleavage of UpA dinucleotides may potentially account for the suppression of UpA dinucleotide frequencies in viral RNA sequences.
source: This may potentially account for the suppression of UpA dinucleotide frequencies in viral RNA sequences.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying UpA suppression.

claim: For E7 the UpU O/E ratio is 1.04.
source: However, this does not explain why viruses have not evolved to under-represent UpU dinucleotides as well as UpA - for E7 the UpU O/E ratio is 1.04.
evidence: This is a factual statement about E7 composition.

claim: Inhibition of IRF3 had no effect on the attenuation of CpG- or UpA-high mutants of E7.
source: We have previously shown that inhibition of IRF3, a pathway intermediate that couples PRR recognition to interferon production, had no effect on the attenuation of CpG- or UpA-high mutants of E7, nor was their replication any more affected by the addition of exogenous IFN than WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The replication of CpG- or UpA-high mutants of E7 was not any more affected by the addition of exogenous IFN than WT virus.
source: We have previously shown that inhibition of IRF3, a pathway intermediate that couples PRR recognition to interferon production, had no effect on the attenuation of CpG- or UpA-high mutants of E7, nor was their replication any more affected by the addition of exogenous IFN than WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: None of the currently described PRRs are known to recognise CpGs in RNA sequences.
source: None of the currently described PRRs are known to recognise CpGs in RNA sequences, although CpG dinucleotides in oligodeoxynucleotides or other DNA sequences can activate antiviral gene expression through TLR9 (Hemmi et al., 2000; Dorn and Kippenberger, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about current knowledge in the field.

claim: CpG dinucleotides in oligodeoxynucleotides or other DNA sequences can activate antiviral gene expression through TLR9.
source: None of the currently described PRRs are known to recognise CpGs in RNA sequences, although CpG dinucleotides in oligodeoxynucleotides or other DNA sequences can activate antiviral gene expression through TLR9 (Hemmi et al., 2000; Dorn and Kippenberger, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Removing CpGs from a transgene drastically improved its expression in vivo while at the same time reducing cytokine expression and increasing the persistence of the transgene.
source: In addition, removing CpGs from a transgene drastically improved its expression in vivo while at the same time reducing cytokine expression and increasing the persistence of the transgene (Yew et al., 2002; Hodges et al., 2004; Hyde et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Persistent transgene expression in TLR9 knock out mice still required complete removal of CpG dinucleotides.
source: Although also in this system, TLR9 was shown to be indispensable as persistent transgene expression in TLR9 knock out mice still required complete removal of CpG dinucleotides (Bazzani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There exists a TLR9 independent mechanism that detects CpG dinucleotides in transcripts.
source: Together this indicates the existence of a TLR9 independent mechanism that detects CpG dinucleotides in transcripts.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited literature showing TLR9-independent CpG effects.

claim: GU-rich and AU-rich sequences have been identified as preferential TLR7/8 activator, enhancing cytokine expression of IFN-α and TNFα.
source: GU-rich and AU-rich sequences have been identified as preferential TLR7/8 activator, enhancing cytokine expression of IFN-α and TNFα (Lund et al., 2004; Heil et al., 2004; Diebold et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An additional CpG dinucleotide in an AU-rich context enhances TLR7 mediated cytokine expression.
source: Interestingly, an additional CpG dinucleotide in an AU-rich context enhances TLR7 mediated cytokine expression (Jimenez-Baranda et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The cell types used in this study are not known to express detectable levels of TLR7/8.
source: However, the cell types used in this study are not known to express detectable levels of TLR7/8, nor do increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies in either E7 or influenza viruses upregulate TLR7/8 specific cytokines (Gaunt et al., 2016; Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the cell types used and supported by citations.

claim: Increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies in either E7 or influenza viruses do not upregulate TLR7/8 specific cytokines.
source: However, the cell types used in this study are not known to express detectable levels of TLR7/8, nor do increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies in either E7 or influenza viruses upregulate TLR7/8 specific cytokines (Gaunt et al., 2016; Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is unlikely that TLR7/8 signalling is at the heart of the observed restriction.
source: It is therefore unlikely that TLR7/8 signalling is at the heart of the observed restriction.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of TLR7/8 expression and cytokine upregulation.

claim: The absence of any differences in ISG expression between WT and mutant viruses makes a controlling role for interferon-coupled responses to such mutants highly unlikely.
source: Furthermore, the absence of any differences in ISG expression between WT and mutant viruses (Gaunt et al., 2016; Atkinson et al., 2014) together with the complete lack of any inducible antiviral response to UpA and CpG containing RNA (Figure 10) makes a controlling role for interferon-coupled responses to such mutants highly unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference from cited literature and data in Figure 10.

claim: Picornaviruses are particularly well armoured against IFN-mediated cellular responses.
source: Picornaviruses furthermore are particularly well armoured against IFN-mediated cellular responses that reduces the likelihood of any role in attenuating CpG- or UpA-high mutants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about picornaviruses.

claim: The enterovirus-encoded 2C protease cleaves a variety of host factors (i.e. MAVS, MDA5, RIG-I).
source: The enterovirus-encoded 2C protease cleaves a variety of host factors (i.e. MAVS, MDA5, RIG-I) (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; Barral et al., 2007, 2009) and renders this PRR-linked pathway non-functional during virus replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The enterovirus 2C protease renders the PRR-linked pathway non-functional during virus replication.
source: The enterovirus-encoded 2C protease cleaves a variety of host factors (i.e. MAVS, MDA5, RIG-I) (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; Barral et al., 2007, 2009) and renders this PRR-linked pathway non-functional during virus replication.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited literature about protease function.

claim: E7 replication was relatively insensitive to effects of pre-treating cells with high concentrations of exogenous IFN-α.
source: E7 replication was relatively insensitive to effects of pre-treating cells with high concentrations of exogenous IFN-α, nor were CpG- or UpA-high mutant differentially inhibited (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: CpG- or UpA-high mutants were not differentially inhibited by exogenous IFN-α compared to WT.
source: E7 replication was relatively insensitive to effects of pre-treating cells with high concentrations of exogenous IFN-α, nor were CpG- or UpA-high mutant differentially inhibited (Atkinson et al., 2014).
